summary: The Histories, written in the fifth century BC by Herodotus of Halicarnassus, is the founding work of Western history. Its stated aim is to keep the deeds of Greeks and non-Greeks from being forgotten, and to explain why they went to war. Herodotus follows the rise of the Persian Empire through Lydia, Babylon and Egypt, then the Greek resistance at Marathon and Thermopylae. He mixes eyewitness report, hearsay, geography, customs and story, and often says when he doubts what he was told.
context: Herodotus lived about 484 to 425 BC. He says he travelled widely, interviewing people and collecting stories, mostly in territories of the Persian Empire. He presents the conflict as one of Persian slavery against Greek freedom, though the account is not impartial. Later editors split the work into nine books named for the Muses. The oldest surviving manuscripts date from the 9th and 10th centuries AD. This edition is G. C. Macaulay's English translation, about 288,000 words, from Standard Ebooks.

sources.title: The Histories, translated by G. C. Macaulay (Standard Ebooks)

people.name: Herodotus
people.note: Born about 484 BC at Halicarnassus; counted as the first Western historian and the source of almost everything the book reports.

people.name: Croesus
people.note: Rules the nations west of the river Halys, tests the oracles, and is defeated by Cyrus before becoming his advisor.

people.name: Solon
people.note: Answers Croesus's question about the happiest man, and tells him to look to the end of every matter.

people.name: Cyrus II of Persia
people.note: Conquers Lydia and Babylon and dies attacking the Massagetae.

people.name: Cambyses II
people.note: Son of Cyrus; attacks Egypt and defeats Psammetichus III, then his madness is described.

people.name: Xerxes
people.note: Succeeds Darius, bridges the Hellespont, and marches against Greece.

people.name: Leonidas I
people.note: Leads the small Greek force sent to hold Thermopylae against the Persian army.

people.name: Dienekes
people.note: His sayings are recorded at Thermopylae, including a joke about fighting in the shade.

people.name: Gyges
people.note: Seizes the Lydian kingdom after the king makes him see his wife naked.

people.name: Themistocles
people.note: Is paid thirty talents in the account of the fleet's stand in front of Euboea.

places.name: Halicarnassus
places.note: Herodotus's home city, named in the first sentence of the book.

places.name: Babylon
places.note: Assyrian city whose design and ways are described before Cyrus attacks it.

places.name: Giza
places.note: Site of the Great Pyramid, which Cheops builds with machines, in the account of Egypt.

places.name: Delphi
places.note: Oracle that tells Croesus that if he attacks, a great empire will fall.

places.name: Marathon
places.note: Athenian victory under Miltiades that spurs Darius to raise a new army.

places.name: Thermopylae
places.note: Pass where Leonidas's small force is sent to delay the Persians.

places.name: Hellespont
places.note: Strait that Xerxes crosses with a pontoon bridge, and in anger has lashed.

places.name: Plataea
places.note: Town whose alliance with Athens is explained; the summary of Book VI notes its help to Athens.

timeline.label: Thales predicts the solar eclipse of 28 May, which falls during the Battle of Halys.
Herodotus is born, by the conventional dating c. 484 BC.
Herodotus dies, by the conventional dating c. 425 BC.
The oldest surviving copies of the Histories are Byzantine manuscripts of the 9th and 10th centuries.

ideas.title: Inquiry as the aim
ideas.note: The word historia means enquiry; the stated purpose is to stop deeds from fading and to explain the cause of the war.

ideas.title: Freedom against empire
ideas.note: Persian despotism is set against the Greek city-states, though Herodotus does not make Greeks all heroes.

ideas.title: Fortune turns
ideas.note: Solon tells Croesus to look to the end of every matter and that the Deity is altogether envious.

ideas.title: Customs and difference
ideas.note: Long sections on Egypt, Babylon and Scythia show peoples by their own laws, an early comparative ethnography.

ideas.title: Hubris of kings
ideas.note: Xerxes has the sea whipped and fettered; Herodotus reports it with distance and says he heard it said.

passages.quote: Showing forth of the Inquiry of Herodotus of Halicarnassos, to the end that neither the deeds of men may be forgotten by lapse of time, nor the works great and marvellous, which have been produced some by Hellenes and some by Barbarians, may lose their renown;
passages.why: The opening statement of purpose: keep great deeds from fading and explain the war.

passages.quote: the Deity is altogether envious and apt to disturb our lot. For in the course of long time a man may see many things which he would not desire to see, and suffer also many things which he would not desire to suffer. The limit of life for a man I lay down at seventy years:
passages.why: Solon's reply to Croesus, a plain statement of how fortune turns.

passages.quote: since the time when Psammetichos having become king desired to know what men had come into being first, they suppose that the Phrygians came into being before themselves, but they themselves before all other men.
passages.why: The experiment to find the oldest people, an early test by observation.

passages.quote: bade them scourge the Hellespont with three hundred strokes of the lash and let down into the sea a pair of fetters. Nay, I have heard further that he sent branders also with them to brand the Hellespont. However this may be, he enjoined them, as they were beating, to say Barbarian and presumptuous words as follows:
passages.why: Xerxes's anger at the sea, reported with a historian's caveat.

passages.quote: Thou bitter water, thy master lays upon thee this penalty, because thou didst wrong him not having suffered any wrong from him: and Xerxes the king will pass over thee whether thou be willing or no; but with right, as it seems, no man doeth sacrifice to thee, seeing that thou art a treacherous and briny stream.”
passages.why: The words said to the Hellespont as it is scourged.

passages.quote: he said that their guest from Trachis brought them very good news, for if the Medes obscured the light of the sun, the battle against them would be in the shade and not in the sun. 227.
